# Who Owns the Archive? — finished platform kit

## 1. LONG VIDEO
Open the archive door and refuse the singular noun. Follow one Worth dress through object title, house attribution, designer credit, donor history, accession, image status, and museum custody. Then build the rights constellation without pretending the object record answers private contracts or title disputes.

## 2. SHORT 01
“Owning the garment is not automatically owning every photograph, sketch, story, or copyright around it.” Show six separate evidence lanes.

## 3. SHORT 02
“The archive is a room. Ownership is a map.” Every asserted verb—hold, copy, lend, publish, sell, destroy—must point to a record.

## 4. CAROUSEL
WHO OWNS THE ARCHIVE? / WHICH ITEM? / PHYSICAL TITLE / COPYRIGHT / CONTRACT / PRIVACY / ACCESS / CONSERVATION / INTERPRETATION / COUNSEL GATE.

## 5. NEWSLETTER
Subject: The archive does not have one owner just because it has one address. Walk readers through the ten-item audit and the difference between custody and underlying rights.

## 6. REGISTRAR EDITION
A field-by-field transfer checklist for identifier, origin, condition, rights evidence, restrictions, files, checksums, context, and correction history.

## Claim ledger
- **VERIFIED:** Under U.S. law, ownership of a material object is distinct from ownership of copyright embodied in it. (S63)
- **INFERENCE:** An archive may contain garments, photographs, drawings, recordings, files, marks, contracts, and access credentials governed by different records and jurisdictions. (S63, S08, S39)
- **INFERENCE:** Possession of the storage room or server does not by itself establish every underlying right. (S63)

## Publication discipline
Do not invent production arrangements or add unlicensed imagery. Preserve captions, alt text, creator and institution credits, canonical URLs, evidence labels, labor and jurisdiction limits, participant correction, and counsel or specialist gates.
